texts.exact_text: Kwâi requires (in him who would fulfil its meaning) the exhibition (of the culprit's guilt) in the royal court, and a sincere and earnest appeal (for sympathy and support), with a consciousness of the peril (involved in cutting off the criminal). He should (also) make announcement in his own city, and show that it will not be well to have recourse at once to arms. (In this way) there will be advantage in whatever he shall go forward to.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject in (the pride of) strength advancing with his toes. He goes forward, but will not succeed. There will be ground for blame.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject full of apprehension and appealing (for sympathy and help). Late at night hostile measures may be (taken against him), but he need not be anxious about them.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject (about to advance) with strong (and determined) looks. There will be evil. (But) the superior man, bent on cutting off (the criminal), will walk alone and encounter the rain, (till he be hated by his proper associates) as if he were contaminated (by the others). (In the end) there will be no blame against him.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows one from whose buttocks the skin has been stripped, and who walks slowly and with difficulty. (If he could act) like. a sheep led (after its companions), occasion for repentance would disappear. But though he hear these words, he will not believe them.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows (the small men like) a bed of purslain, which ought to be uprooted with the utmost determination. (The subject of the line having such determination), his action, in harmony with his central position, will lead to no error or blame.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth SIX, divided, shows its subject without any (helpers) on whom to call. His end will be evil.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, line 6

texts.exact_text:
In Kwâi we have the hexagram of the third month, when the last remnant, cold and dark, of winter, represented by the sixth line, is about to disappear before the advance of the warm and bright days of the approaching summer. In the yīn line at the top king Wén saw the symbol of a small or bad man, a feudal prince or high minister, lending his power to maintain a corrupt government, or, it might be, a dynasty that was waxen old and ready to vanish away; and in the five undivided lines he saw the representatives of good order, or, it might be, the dynasty which was to supersede the other. This then is the subject of the hexagram, -- how bad men, statesmen corrupt and yet powerful, are to be put out of the way. And he who would accomplish the task must do so by the force of his character more than by force of arms, and by producing a general sympathy on his side.

The Tuàn says that he must openly denounce the criminal in the court, seek to awaken general sympathy, and at the same time go about his enterprise, conscious of its difficulty and danger. Among his own adherents, moreover, as if it were in his own city, he must make it understood how unwillingly he takes up arms. Then let him go forward, and success will attend him.

Line 1 is strong, the first line of that trigram, which expresses the idea of strength. But it is in the lowest place. The stage of the enterprise is too early, and the preparation too small to make victory certain. Its subject had better not take the field.

Line 2 is strong, and central, and its subject is possessed with the determination to do his part in the work of removal. But his eagerness is tempered by his occupancy of an even place; and he is cautious, and no attempts, however artful, to harm him will take effect.

Line 3 is strong, and its subject displays his purpose too eagerly. Being beyond the central position, moreover, gives an indication of evil. Lines 3 and 6 are also proper correlates; and, as elsewhere in the Yì Jīng, the meeting of yīn and yáng lines is associated with falling rain. The subject of 3, therefore, communicates with 6, in a way that annoys his associates; but nevertheless he commits no error, and, in the end, incurs no blame.

Line 4 is not in the centre, nor in an odd place, appropriate to it as undivided. Its subject therefore will not be at rest, nor able to do anything to accomplish the idea of the hexagram. He is symbolised by a culprit, who, according to the ancient and modern custom of Chinese courts, has been bastinadoed till he presents the appearance in the Text. Alone he can do nothing; if he could follow others, like a sheep led along, he might accomplish something, but he will not listen to advice.

Purslain grows in shady places, and hence we find it here in close contiguity to the topmost line, which is yīn. As 5 is the ruler's seat, evil may come to him from such contiguity, and strenuous efforts must be made to prevent such an evil. The subject of the line, the ruler in the central place, will commit no error. It must be allowed that the symbolism in this line is not easily managed.

The subject of the 6th line, standing alone, may be easily disposed of. 夬 ䷪
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 43; scan-backed transcription p. 151, notes

texts.exact_text: 夬：揚于王庭，孚號，有厲，告自邑，不利即戎，利有攸往。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 夬，決也，剛決柔也。健而說，決而和，揚于王庭，柔乘五剛也。孚號有厲，其危乃光也。告自邑，不利即戎，所尚乃窮也。利有攸往，剛長乃終也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 彖

texts.exact_text: 澤上于天，夬；君子以施祿及下，居德則忌。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初九：壯于前趾，往不勝為咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 不勝而往，咎也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 九二：惕號，莫夜有戎，勿恤。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 莫夜有戎，得中道也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 九三：壯于頄，有凶。君子夬夬，獨行遇雨，若濡有慍，无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 君子夬夬，終无咎也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 九四：臀无膚，其行次且。牽羊悔亡，聞言不信。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 其行次且，位不當也。聞言不信，聰不明也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 九五：莧陸夬夬，中行无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 中行无咎，中未光也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上六：无號，終有凶。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 无號之凶，終不可長也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/夬; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 43, 小象 6

texts.exact_text:
Kwâi is the symbol of displacing or removing. We see (in the figure) the strong (lines) displacing the weak. (We have in it the attributes of) strength and complacency. There is displacement, but harmony (continues).

'The exhibition (of the criminal's guilt) in the royal courtyard' is suggested by the (one) weak (line) mounted on the five strong lines. There 'is an earnest and sincere appeal (for sympathy and support), and a consciousness of the peril (involved in the undertaking):' -- it is the realisation of this danger, which makes the method (of compassing the object) brilliant. 'He should make an announcement in his own city, and show that it will not be well to have recourse at once to arms:' -- (if he have recourse to arms), what he prefers will (soon) be exhausted. 'There will be advantage in whatever he shall go forward to:' -- when the growth of the strong (lines) has been completed, there will be an end (of the displacement).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 43, p. 250

texts.exact_text: (The trigram ☰ representing) heaven and ☱ that for the waters of a marsh mounting above it form Kwâi. The superior man, in accordance with this, bestows emolument on those below him, and dislikes allowing his gifts to accumulate (undispensed).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, p. 321

texts.exact_text: 'Without (being able to) succeed, he goes forward:' -- this is an error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, line 1, p. 321

texts.exact_text: 'Though hostile measures be taken against him, he need not be anxious:' -- he pursues the course of the due mean.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, line 2, p. 321

texts.exact_text: 'The superior man looks bent on cutting off the culprit:' -- there will in the end be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, line 3, p. 321

texts.exact_text: 'He walks slowly and with difficulty:' -- he is not in the place appropriate to him.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, line 4, p. 321

texts.exact_text: 'If his action be in harmony with his central position, there will be no error:' -- but his standing in the due mean is not yet clearly displayed.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, line 5, p. 321

texts.exact_text: 'There is the misery of having none on whom to call:' -- the end will be that he cannot continue any longer.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 43, line 6, p. 321
